segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with the rainbow over his head; his face was like the sun, and his legs were like pillars of fire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He held in his hand a little scroll that lay open. He set his right foot on the sea and his left on the land,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he cried out with a loud voice, as a lion roars. And when he cried out, the seven thunders spoke in their own voices.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when the seven thunders had spoken, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Seal up what the seven thunders said, and do not write it down.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the angel whom I had seen standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and swore by the one who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it:

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: but in the days of the sound of the seventh angel, when he is about to blow his trumpet, the secret of God will be brought to completion, just as he announced the good news to his own slaves the prophets.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke with me again and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Go, take the scroll that lies open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Take it and eat it up. It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I took the little scroll from the angel’s hand and ate it up, and in my mouth it was sweet as honey; but when I had eaten it, my stomach was made bitter.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You must prophesy again about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.”

notes.note: The Greek word normally means “foot,” and it is translated that way in verse 2, where the angel plants one on the sea and one on the land. Here the comparison to pillars shows that the whole limb is in view, a wider use the word allows, so most modern versions say “legs.” Older versions keep “feet.”

The Greek has the definite article, as if these thunders were already known to the reader, though the book has not mentioned them before. Many interpreters see an echo of Psalm 29, where “the voice of the Lord” thunders seven times. That link is plausible but not certain.

notes.phrase: There will be no more delay
notes.traditional: there should be time no longer
notes.note: The Greek is literally “time will no longer be.” Older versions took this to mean that time itself would cease. Most scholars now read the word as “an interval” or “delay,” because the next clause says what happens instead: God’s purpose is completed without further waiting. The scene, with a hand raised to heaven and an oath by the one who lives forever, echoes Daniel 12:7, where the question is how long it will be until the end.

Most English versions keep “mystery,” treating it as a technical term for a truth once hidden and now revealed. In Jewish Greek of the period the word was the ordinary term for a secret, especially God’s hidden plan that only he can disclose. English “mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something unknowable, which is not the point here.

Most versions say only that God “announced” or “declared” this to the prophets. The verb is the one elsewhere translated “preach the gospel,” an ordinary word for bringing good news. The translation keeps that sense visible: the completion of God’s secret plan is presented as good news.

Nearly all English versions have “his servants the prophets,” a phrase familiar from the Old Testament. The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, someone who belongs to a master, not a hired servant. In Jewish usage, to be called God’s slave was a title of honor, borne by Moses and the prophets.

The scene is modeled on the call of the prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3), who is told to eat a scroll of God’s words and finds it sweet as honey in his mouth. The bitterness in the stomach is John’s own addition. It is usually taken to reflect the painful content of the message he must deliver.

The preposition can mean “about,” “against,” or “in the presence of.” Older versions have “before,” and some interpreters prefer “against,” since the prophecies that follow are largely judgments. “About” is the most common modern rendering and leaves the tone open.

This is the same Greek word that is translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in the New Testament, where it means the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation’s repeated lists of peoples, nations, and languages, the scope is all the peoples of the world, so “nations” is used.

candidates.reason: It occurs across the whole New Testament, and translators split between “slave,” “servant,” and “bondservant,” so a reader would be misled if the word changed from chapter to chapter.

Versions alternate between “book” and “scroll” (and “certificate” or “record” elsewhere), and Revelation’s imagery depends on a consistent choice, including the diminutive βιβλαρίδιον as “little scroll.”
The traditional “tongues” is archaic for the sense “languages,” and the choice affects Acts 2, 1 Corinthians 12–14, and Revelation’s repeated lists of peoples.
It is rendered “belly,” “stomach,” “womb,” or “heart” in different places (John 7:38, Philippians 3:19, the birth narratives), so the senses need a fixed rendering each.
